The Striated thornbill, weighing just 7.5 grams [Wwi = 7.5 grams] as an adult female, is one of the smallest insectivorous passerines in the woodlands of southeastern Australia. Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at 31 °C [T = 31 °C] after approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], though the incubation period can range from 11 to 17 days depending on ambient conditions. At hatching, these altricial nestlings weigh only 1.32 grams [Ww0 = 1.32 grams], reflecting the extremely limited yolk reserves typical of small passerines. The parents initiate intensive brooding and provisioning almost immediately, as the naked, blind chicks are entirely dependent on exogenous heat and food. The rapid growth phase that follows is fueled by a diet of small arthropods, primarily spiders and leafhoppers, gleaned from the foliage of eucalypts. This early developmental trajectory, from a minute hatchling to a fully feathered fledgling, is remarkably compressed in this species, requiring sustained parental effort to ensure the nestlings reach critical mass before departing the nest.

This value, obtained from standard respirometry trials, aligns closely with predictions derived from allometric equations for passerines of similar body mass, suggesting no extraordinary metabolic adaptation. The elevated temperature at which measurements were taken corresponds to the upper range of active body temperatures recorded during foraging bouts in the field. Such a metabolic profile is consistent with a high-energy lifestyle centered on continuous insect pursuit, rather than energy-conserving strategies seen in more sedentary species. The data highlight that even at rest, the Striated thornbill maintains a relatively high metabolic rate, presumably to sustain its rapid digestion and constant readiness for flight.

Once the juvenile leaves the nest, it remains dependent on parental provisioning for another two to three weeks, during which it refines its foraging skills on small prey. The early independence from the nest is balanced by an extended post-fledging care phase, which increases the likelihood of survival during the vulnerable initial weeks. The timing of nest departure appears tightly linked to wing feather development: chicks that achieve a critical pin-feather length tend to fledge earlier, while those with slower growth may remain in the nest an extra day.

However, first reproduction is typically deferred until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], as young birds must first establish a territory and accumulate sufficient energy reserves for the demands of egg production and nestling care at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Females that delay their first clutch to the following austral spring show higher fledging success than those attempting to breed in their hatching year. Longevity records for the Striated thornbill indicate a maximum lifespan of 4307 days [am = 4307 days] when measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], representing approximately 11.8 years of sustained activity in the wild. This extended survival, unusual for such a diminutive passerine, is likely facilitated by its robust anti-predator behaviors and a generalist foraging strategy that buffers against seasonal fluctuations in arthropod availability. The species exhibits low annual adult mortality, and banding studies in the forests of Victoria have recovered individuals well into their second decade. This life-history pattern, combining a high metabolic rate with remarkable longevity, challenges the conventional expectation that small body size necessarily correlates with short lifespans.
